title: Case Studies – Topic 1.2 Development and the Global Economy
file: 3b Case Studies – Topic 1.2 Development and the Global Economy
intro: One real case (2015 or later) for each case-study slot in H2 Topic 1.2. A slot is a syllabus content point that asks for a variation, trend, factor, characteristic, impact or actor. Where the syllabus asks how far an actor can influence others, the slot has a pair: a strong and a limited case, or one that succeeded and one that failed.
Each case is about 1 page, with 1 chart drawn from its sources. The 'Links' line under each case shows other slots and topics where the same case can be used, including cases in doc 3a (Topic 1.1).

cases.heading: 1.2.1 Development — Variations (across space)
cases.syllabus: Variations across space in levels of development between macro-regions, countries within a macro-region, and different places within a country.
facts: Singapore's HDI (0.949) is far above Cambodia's (0.600), and 9th in the world
cases.caption: Figure 1. Human Development Index of ASEAN members, 2022 data (UNDP report, via Katadata).

sections.title: What it shows
sections.text: Southeast Asia as a macro-region sits in the middle of the world's development range, but the gaps inside it are wide. Four members have very high HDI, three high and three medium. The gaps repeat inside countries: in Indonesia, Jakarta's HDI was 84.15 in 2024, the highest of 38 provinces, while Papua scored 61.39 in 2022.

sections.title: How it shows variations at three scales
bullets: Macro-region: Southeast Asia overall is a middle-income region, behind East Asia's richest economies.
Countries within the region: Singapore (0.949) ranks 9th in the world. Cambodia (0.600), Myanmar (0.608) and Laos (0.620) are in the medium group.
Places within a country: Jakarta, the capital and business hub, scores far above remote Papua, where services and jobs are thinner.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: Use the same indicator (HDI) at all three scales to show that variation is found at every scale.
Evaluation: Indonesia's provincial figures use a national (BPS) method that changed in 2024, so compare them only within one method.

cases.links: Links: 1.2.1 flows and development (Vietnam, slot 2) · 1.1.1 measuring progress with indicators (3a slot 3) · 3.1.1 measuring SUD.

cases.heading: 1.2.1 Development — Trends (flows of trade and capital)
cases.syllabus: Global patterns of flows of trade, capital and labour: unevenness and shifts; their influence on variations in development.
facts: Vietnam (northern electronics clusters, southern industrial zones)
Record US$36.6 billion of FDI in 2023; foreign-invested firms make about 72% of exports
Samsung and other Korean, Japanese, Taiwanese and Singaporean TNCs; Vietnamese government
cases.caption: Figure 2. Falling poverty and the foreign share of Vietnam's exports (various sources; see list).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: As costs rose in China and trade tensions grew, investors added factories in Vietnam ('regionalisation' of supply chains). FDI reached a record US$36.6 billion in 2023. Samsung alone made about US$54 billion of exports in 2024, about 13% of the total, and Korean firms together about 30% in 2023.

sections.title: How it shows the trend
bullets: Shift: flows of capital moved towards Vietnam, so trade flows from it grew too. This is part of the shift of manufacturing within Asia.
Unevenness: flows are concentrated. Foreign firms make nearly three-quarters of exports, and a few TNCs dominate.
Influence on development: the national poverty rate fell from 14% (2010) to 5.7% (2023), and extreme poverty fell below 1% by 2020.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: Flows and development feed each other: Vietnam's low costs attracted FDI, and FDI raised incomes.
Evaluation: dependence on a few foreign firms and on US markets is a risk; new US tariffs of up to 46% threatened the model in 2025.

cases.links: Links: 1.2.1 shift towards manufacturing (slot 4) · 1.2.2 impacts on host economies (slot 8) · 3a slot 9 (Vietnam's solar boom).

cases.heading: 1.2.1 Development — Factors (development shapes flows)
cases.syllabus: Influence of variations in levels of development on global flows of labour (and of these flows on development).
facts: Philippines and its workers in the US, Singapore, Saudi Arabia and elsewhere
Record US$38.34 billion in remittances in 2024, 8.3% of GDP; 4th-largest receiver in the world
Overseas Filipino workers (land- and sea-based), their families, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
cases.caption: Figure 3. Where Philippine cash remittances came from in 2024 (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Millions of Filipinos work abroad, on land and at sea. In 2024 they sent home a record US$38.34 billion, up 3% from US$37.21 billion in 2023. December 2024 alone brought a monthly record of US$3.73 billion.

sections.title: How it shows the factors
bullets: Development shapes the flow: higher wages and jobs in richer places (the US, Singapore, the Gulf) pull workers from a lower-income country.
The flow shapes development: remittances equal 8.3% of GDP and drive household spending on housing, education, cars and investment.
Conditions abroad matter: economists linked the 2024 rise to recovery and higher wages in host economies, plus a weaker peso.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: Development gaps cause labour flows, and those flows narrow some gaps for households at home.
Evaluation: dependence on remittances ties the Philippines to other economies' cycles; the brain drain of nurses and seafarers is a cost.

cases.links: Links: 1.2.2 interdependence through labour flows (slot 6) · 1.2.3 labour as an actor · 3a slot 7 (West African fishers migrating).

cases.heading: 1.2.1 Development — Trends (towards manufacturing)
cases.syllabus: Shifts in global production since the 1950s: likely shift towards manufacturing and a decrease in the share of agriculture for some countries.
facts: Ethiopia: Hawassa, Mekelle, Bole Lemi industrial parks
Hawassa opened July 2016; AGOA suspension January 2022
Agriculture fell from 58.7% of GDP (1991) to 33.8% (2017); farming still employs about 60% of workers
Ethiopian government, foreign apparel firms, US government (AGOA trade preferences)
cases.caption: Figure 4. Hawassa's jobs vs plan, and jobs lost after the US suspended AGOA (National Bank of Ethiopia).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Ethiopia built industrial parks to pull workers out of farming into export manufacturing. Hawassa, Africa's largest textile and apparel park, opened in 2016 with a target of 60,000 jobs and US$1 billion a year in exports. The US suspended Ethiopia from AGOA's duty-free access in January 2022 over the conflict in the north.

sections.title: How it shows the trend
bullets: Shift away from agriculture: farming's share of GDP has fallen for decades, though about 60% of workers are still in it (2025).
Shift towards manufacturing is fragile: Hawassa employed about 28,000 in 2023, under half the target, and earned US$114 million in exports in 2021.
Exposure to global decisions: after AGOA was suspended, about 11,500 park jobs were lost (4,321 at Hawassa) and park exports fell 24% in 2023.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: The 'likely shift' to manufacturing depends on access to markets and TNC decisions, not just cheap labour.
Evaluation: manufacturing's share of GDP stayed near 5–6%, so Ethiopia shows the shift can stall.

cases.heading: 1.2.1 Development — Trends (towards services)
cases.syllabus: Likely shift towards the service sector for countries at higher levels of development as the competitiveness of their manufacturing sector declines.
facts: China; low-end factories moving to Vietnam, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Myanmar
Services rose from 44% to 53% of China's economic activity in a decade (World Bank)
Chinese government, TNCs and their contract manufacturers, garment and footwear buyers
cases.caption: Figure 5. China's services share and the rise of its low-cost rivals (World Bank; Fitch via Business Standard).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: As China grew richer, wages, land costs and the yuan all rose. Fitch said China's wages had passed those of other emerging economies in the region, so labour-intensive industries began to move. Meanwhile services such as retail, finance and digital platforms grew faster than industry.

sections.title: How it shows the trend
bullets: Towards services: services grew from 44% to 53% of economic activity over a decade.
Manufacturing competitiveness fell at the low end: an estimated 25–35% of China's clothing export value shifted out.
Where it went: Bangladesh and Vietnam's share of world clothing, footwear and furniture exports rose from 3% (2010) to 8% (2015).

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: One shift drives another: China's move to services is the other side of the move to manufacturing in poorer countries (slots 2 and 4).
Evaluation: China kept high-tech manufacturing, so its competitiveness fell only in labour-intensive goods.

cases.heading: 1.2.2 Global Economy and TNCs — Impacts (interdependence)
cases.syllabus: The connections and interdependence between places in the global economy as a result of trade, capital and labour flows.
facts: Chip plants in Taiwan and Malaysia; car plants worldwide
7.7 million vehicles not built and US$210 billion of car-industry revenue lost in 2021 (forecast)
Carmakers, chipmakers (e.g. TSMC), chip packaging plants in Malaysia, governments
cases.caption: Figure 6. AlixPartners' forecasts of what the chip shortage cost carmakers in 2021.

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Carmakers cut chip orders early in the pandemic, then demand bounced back while chipmakers were serving booming electronics sales. In mid-2021 a COVID outbreak in Malaysia closed chip assembly, test and packaging plants. AlixPartners nearly doubled its forecast of lost car revenue, from US$110 billion (May) to US$210 billion (September 2021).

sections.title: How it shows interdependence
bullets: Connections: a car built in Germany or the US relies on chips made in Taiwan and packaged in Malaysia.
Shock travels along the flows: a lockdown in one country stopped car lines in many others, with 7.7 million vehicles not built in 2021.
Not just chips: the same forecast listed resin and steel shortages, so many flows were strained at once.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: Interdependence brings efficiency in normal times and fragility in a crisis.
Evaluation: it pushed states to subsidise local chip plants, e.g. TSMC in Arizona (slot 11).

cases.links: Links: 1.2.3 labour characteristics (TSMC Arizona, slot 11) · 1.2.2 GPNs (slot 7) · 1.2.3 states and TNCs.

cases.heading: 1.2.2 Global Economy and TNCs — Characteristics (how a GPN connects places)
cases.case: Apple's iPhone network and the move to India (2023–2025)
cases.syllabus: Ways by which GPNs of TNCs connect places through flows of materials and capital: sourcing of inputs, transformation into products, distribution and consumption in different places.
facts: Design in the US; assembly in China and India (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka); sales worldwide
Apple makes about 220–230 million iPhones a year; about 55 million were assembled in India in 2025
Apple (lead firm), contract assemblers Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron, component suppliers, Indian government
cases.caption: Figure 7. iPhones assembled in India (Bloomberg, via Business Today and others).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Apple designs iPhones in the US but owns no assembly plants. Contract makers assemble them, mostly in China. Since 2023 Apple has moved more assembly to India: output there rose about 53% to roughly 55 million in 2025, about a quarter of the total. All iPhone 17 models, including the Pro, are now assembled in India too.

sections.title: How the GPN connects places
bullets: Sourcing: parts come from many suppliers; Apple is now adding Indian suppliers for battery cells, casings and accessories.
Transformation: assembly by Foxconn (over 70% of India's iPhone shipments), Tata Electronics (including a Tamil Nadu site) and Pegatron.
Distribution and consumption: India's factories serve the home market and exports (over US$10 billion of exports in FY2024), while China remains the largest producer.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: A lead firm can reshape the network by moving one stage (assembly) without owning any factories.
Evaluation: estimates of India's share range from about 16% to 25% depending on source and period; quote the range.

cases.links: Links: 1.2.1 China's shift (slot 5) · 1.2.2 impacts on host economies (slot 8) · 1.2.3 states and TNCs (slot 10).

cases.heading: 1.2.2 Global Economy and TNCs — Impacts (host economy)
cases.syllabus: Positive and negative impacts of GPNs of TNCs on host economies: economic, environmental and social.
facts: Bangladesh, especially Dhaka, Gazipur and the Buriganga and Turag rivers
About 3,500 factories, 4 million workers (mostly women), about 85% of exports; world's 2nd-largest apparel exporter (2024)
Global fashion brands, local factory owners, workers and unions, Accord on Fire and Building Safety, government
cases.caption: Figure 8. The 2023 minimum wage dispute, and pollution outlets into Dhaka's rivers (Dhaka Tribune survey).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Global brands source clothes from Bangladeshi factories, linking the country into fashion GPNs. Garment exports reached US$38.48 billion in 2024. After the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse, brands and unions signed the Accord; by 2016 it had inspected 1,600 factories.

sections.title: How it shows the impacts
bullets: Economic (+): millions of jobs and about 85% of export earnings. (−): heavy dependence on one industry and on buyers' prices.

Social (+): paid work for 4 million mostly female workers and, through the Accord, safer buildings. (−): low pay; in 2023 the government set the minimum wage at Tk 12,500 against workers' demand of Tk 20,390, and at least two workers died in protests.
Environmental (−): dyeing and washing plants discharge into rivers; a survey counted 224 pollution outlets into the Buriganga and Turag, with industrial waste 55% of the pollution.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: The same GPN brings both development and harm; who gains depends on bargaining power along the chain.
Evaluation: the Accord shows brands can raise standards when bound by a legal agreement; pay and pollution lag behind.

cases.heading: 1.2.2 Global Economy and TNCs — Impacts (home economy)
cases.syllabus: Positive and negative impacts of GPNs of TNCs on home economies: economic, environmental and social.
facts: Home: Malmesbury, England. Hosts: Malaysia, Singapore
About 3,500 UK staff before 1,000 UK jobs were cut in 2024
Dyson (founded in the UK), UK workers, Malmesbury community, Asian host governments
cases.caption: Figure 9. How Dyson's network moved away from its home base (dates in labels).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Dyson began moving manufacturing from Malmesbury to Malaysia in 2002 and opened a Singapore plant for digital motors in 2013. In 2019 it moved its head office to Singapore, to be near its factories and Asian customers. In 2024 it cut about 1,000 UK jobs, more than a quarter of its British staff.

sections.title: How it shows the home impacts
bullets: Negative (economic, social): factory jobs left long ago; the 2024 cuts hit the UK workforce, and the head office and its decisions are now abroad.
Positive (economic): the UK kept the high-value stage. Malmesbury remains the R&D base, with the Dyson Institute training engineers.
Mixed signal: Dyson said the 2024 cuts were not about moving jobs to cheaper countries, showing home impacts can come from wider restructuring.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: Home economies often keep design and R&D while losing production: a 'hollowing out' with high-skill gains.
Evaluation: when a TNC moves its head office too, even the home country's control over the GPN weakens.

cases.heading: 1.2.3 Actors — States as regulators: STRONG INFLUENCE
cases.case: India bans TikTok and other Chinese apps (2020)
cases.syllabus: Influence of states on TNCs' operations as regulators of economic activities; varying degree of states' influence.
facts: 59 apps banned at once, then 47 clones; about 267 Chinese apps banned in total
Government of India (IT ministry), ByteDance (TikTok's owner), other Chinese TNCs, Indian users
cases.caption: Figure 10a. India's app bans in four numbers.

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: On 15 June 2020, 20 Indian soldiers died in a border clash with China in Ladakh. On 29 June India banned 59 Chinese apps, including TikTok, citing privacy and security: the IT ministry said the apps were 'stealing and surreptitiously transmitting users' data'. Clone apps were banned a month later.

sections.title: How it shows strong influence
bullets: Market access as a lever: a large market lets a state shut a TNC out completely; TikTok's Indian service was suspended.
Regulation tied to security: data-protection and national-security rules gave the legal basis.
Lasting effect: the government stayed firm on the ban, and about 267 Chinese apps were banned in total.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: States with big markets and security concerns can control even the largest TNCs.
Evaluation: analysts called it a geopolitical decision; influence was strong because India could afford to lose the service.

cases.links: Links: 1.2.3 limited state influence (Ireland, next page) · 1.2.2 TNCs and host economies · 3a slot 15 (Indonesia's nickel ban).

cases.heading: 1.2.3 Actors — States as regulators: LIMITED INFLUENCE
cases.syllabus: Influence of states on TNCs' operations as regulators of economic activities; varying degree of states' influence.
facts: EU decision 2016; final court ruling 10 September 2024
€13.1 billion of back taxes plus about €1 billion interest
Apple, Irish government, European Commission, EU Court of Justice
cases.caption: Figure 10b. How concentrated Ireland's corporation tax is (Irish Fiscal Advisory Council, 2024).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: In 2016 the European Commission ruled that Ireland gave Apple illegal state aid through low tax deals. Ireland and Apple both fought the ruling. In September 2024 the EU Court of Justice upheld it, and Ireland had to collect about €13 billion it had argued it was not owed.

sections.title: How it shows limited influence
bullets: Dependence: three groups paid 46% of Ireland's corporation tax in 2024 and the top 10 almost 60%, so Ireland competes to keep TNCs, not to control them.
Rules set elsewhere: the EU, not Ireland, decided Apple's tax, and the OECD's 15% global minimum tax for large firms will raise Ireland's corporation tax take from 2026.
A windfall Ireland did not seek: receipts were about €28 billion in 2024, plus about €11 billion from Apple.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: Small, open states that rely on TNCs have limited influence; their power is shared with blocs such as the EU.
Evaluation: compare with India: market size and dependence explain the varying degree of state influence.

cases.heading: 1.2.3 Actors — Factors (labour characteristics)
cases.syllabus: Influence of labour characteristics on TNCs' locational decisions.
facts: US$40 billion for two fabs (2022), later expanded
TSMC (Taiwanese chipmaker), US government (subsidies), local construction and technical workers, Taiwanese staff
cases.caption: Figure 11. TSMC Arizona from delay to production (dates in labels).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: After the chip shortage, the US paid chipmakers to build at home, and TSMC chose Arizona. In July 2023 it delayed its first fab to 2025 because it could not find enough skilled workers to install the equipment. It sent around 500 experienced Taiwanese staff to install tools and train locals. Trial production began in April 2024, and by early 2025 4 nm chips were in volume production.

sections.title: How it shows labour characteristics
bullets: Skills: specialised installers and technicians were scarce in Arizona, which cost TSMC about a year.
Mobility: TSMC moved skilled labour from Taiwan and needed US visas for them.
Productivity once trained: by October 2024 the fab's usable-chip yield was reported to be about 4 points higher than comparable Taiwan fabs.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: Labour quality, not just cost, shapes where high-tech TNCs locate; here other factors (US policy, customers) won out despite skill gaps.
Evaluation: skill gaps can be fixed over time by training, so labour is a factor that changes, not a fixed one.

cases.links: Links: 1.2.2 chip shortage (slot 6) · 1.2.3 states and TNCs (slot 10) · 1.2.1 China's labour costs (slot 5).

cases.heading: 1.2.3 Actors — Labour unions: SUCCEEDED
cases.syllabus: Influence of labour unions on TNCs and states.
facts: USA: plants of Ford, GM and Stellantis (e.g. Belvidere, Illinois)
Stellantis deal alone covered 43,000 union members
United Auto Workers (UAW), Ford, General Motors, Stellantis
cases.caption: Figure 12a. What the UAW won from Stellantis (AP).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: The UAW struck all three big US carmakers at once but only at chosen plants, adding more as talks stalled (a 'stand-up' strike). Ford settled first, then Stellantis on the same model. The union kept up pressure by walking out at GM's Spring Hill plant.

sections.title: Why the union succeeded
bullets: Pay: 25% general wage rises over 4½ years for top assembly workers (11% at once), about 33% compounded with cost-of-living pay.
Jobs: Stellantis agreed to build a new truck at Belvidere, a plant due to close, rehiring about 1,200 workers plus about 1,000 at a new battery plant.
Tactics: striking all three firms at once, adding plants as talks stalled, kept pressure on each company.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: A strong union in a high-value sector can change a TNC's investment decisions (Belvidere), not just pay.
Evaluation: compare with Amazon (next page): unions win where they are already recognised.

cases.heading: 1.2.3 Actors — Labour unions: FAILED
cases.case: Union votes at Amazon's Bessemer warehouse (2021–2022)
cases.syllabus: Influence of labour unions on TNCs and states.
facts: Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union (RWDSU), Amazon, National Labor Relations Board (NLRB)
cases.caption: Figure 12b. Votes at Bessemer, 2021 and 2022 (union and NLRB figures as reported).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Workers voted against joining the RWDSU in April 2021 by 1,798 to 738. The NLRB then found that Amazon had improperly pressured workers, for example with a company mailbox in view of security cameras, and ordered a new vote. The 2022 re-run was 993 against and 875 for, with 416 ballots challenged.

sections.title: Why the union failed
bullets: TNC power: Amazon campaigned against the union and said 'we don't think unions are the best answer for our employees'.
Weak position: with no recognised union, organisers had to win over thousands of workers while the company campaigned inside the warehouse.
Slow regulation: the labour board's ruling came months later and did not deliver a union.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: Unions struggle to influence TNCs where they lack recognition; the state's labour rules shape the contest.
Evaluation: a different Amazon warehouse (JFK8, Staten Island) voted to unionise in April 2022, 2,654 to 2,131, so failure was not total.

cases.heading: 1.2.3 Actors — States and TNCs shaping labour
cases.syllabus: Influence of TNCs and states on labour: regulation of labour by states; impact of TNCs' decisions on labour.
facts: More than 70,000 delivery riders and ride-hail drivers
Government (Ministry of Manpower), platform firms Grab, Gojek and foodpanda, platform workers and their associations
cases.caption: Figure 13. What Singapore's Platform Workers Act does.

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Platform firms treat riders and drivers as self-employed, so they lacked an employee's savings and injury protection. Singapore created a new legal class, 'platform worker', with set protections that platform operators must provide.

sections.title: How it shows states and TNCs shaping labour
bullets: State regulation: CPF contributions are compulsory for platform workers born in 1995 or later, with the operator paying a share; older workers may opt in.
Injury cover: operators must give work-injury compensation at the same level as employees, while workers are on a job.
TNC decisions still matter: platforms set pay and work allocation through their apps, and some riders disliked giving more of their earnings to CPF.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: A state can reshape a TNC's labour model without banning it, a middle path between letting gig work run freely and treating gig workers as employees.
Evaluation: protection is partial; injury cover applies only while on a job, and the government gave transition support to offset the higher CPF share in 2025.

cases.heading: 1.2.3 Actors — Multilateral institutions: ASEAN
cases.syllabus: Influence of multilateral institutions on TNCs and states: ASEAN.
facts: 10 ASEAN members plus China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand
2.2 billion people and US$38 trillion of GDP, about a third of the world economy
ASEAN (convenor), member governments, TNCs with regional supply chains
cases.caption: Figure 14. RCEP in four numbers (Enterprise Singapore; ADB).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: ASEAN led negotiations for the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, signed in 2020. It replaced a tangle of separate ASEAN+1 deals with one set of trade rules. It came into force for the first ten members on 1 January 2022.

sections.title: How it shows ASEAN's influence
bullets: On states: members agreed to remove tariffs on about 92% of goods traded between them, mostly within 20 years.
On TNCs: a single rule of origin with regional cumulation lets a firm count parts from any member, making it easier to spread production across the region.
ASEAN at the centre: the bloc convened much bigger economies (China, Japan) into an ASEAN-led framework.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: ASEAN's influence comes from convening and rule-setting, not from enforcement power.
Evaluation: RCEP is shallower than some deals, with many farm products excluded and only regional (not full) cumulation.

cases.heading: 1.2.3 Actors — Multilateral institutions: WTO
cases.case: The WTO and Indonesia's nickel export ban (2019–2022)
cases.syllabus: Influence of multilateral institutions on TNCs and states: WTO.
facts: Ban from January 2020; panel ruling 30 November 2022
Case DS592; Indonesia mines over half the world's nickel
World Trade Organization, European Union, Indonesian government, steel and battery TNCs
cases.caption: Figure 15. The nickel dispute and the WTO's broken appeal stage (dates in labels).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: Indonesia banned raw nickel ore exports from January 2020 to force processing at home (see 3a, slot 15). The EU, whose steelmakers wanted the ore, took the case to the WTO. On 30 November 2022 the panel ruled that the ban and the processing rule broke trade rules, and upheld all the EU's claims.

sections.title: How it shows the WTO's influence
bullets: Rules exist: the panel found Indonesia had not justified the ban as a temporary measure for a critical shortage.
But enforcement failed: Indonesia appealed 'into the void' in December 2022. The Appellate Body has not worked since December 2019, so the ruling could not become final.
States keep control: Indonesia's energy minister said it need not change the rule while the appeal was pending; the EU began exploring countermeasures instead.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: The WTO can judge but cannot always enforce; its influence depends on members accepting the result.
Evaluation: a state with market power (over half of world nickel) can resist a ruling, as India did with the Indus court (3a, slot 12).

cases.heading: 1.2.3 Actors — Multilateral institutions: World Bank
cases.case: The World Bank's Doing Business rankings (2014–2024)
cases.syllabus: Influence of multilateral institutions on TNCs and states: World Bank.
facts: World Bank, national governments, investors and TNCs that used the rankings
cases.caption: Figure 16. India's Doing Business rank, 2014–2019 reports (lower is better).

sections.title: What happened
sections.text: The yearly Doing Business report ranked countries on how easy it was to start and run a firm. Governments reformed rules to climb it: India set a 2015 goal of reaching the top 50 and rose from 142nd to 63rd. In 2021 the World Bank stopped the report after an inquiry found data in the 2018 and 2020 editions had been changed, including to favour China.

sections.title: How it shows the World Bank's influence
bullets: On states: a ranking gave governments a target. India's rise came from changes such as a new insolvency code and faster permits, taxes and electricity connections.
On TNCs: investors used the rankings to compare places, so a better rank was a selling point for FDI.
Loss of trust: the data scandal ended the report, and its replacement B-READY (first edition October 2024) avoids a single league table.

sections.title: Exam angle
bullets: The World Bank shapes states through information and loans, not just money; rankings were a soft but strong lever.
Evaluation: critics said it encouraged a 'race to the bottom' on regulation; influence also depends on the data being trusted.
